I'd like to add to the conversation about injuries. One of the best things you can do to reduce your risk of injuries is to do some form of S&C work off the mats (the more 'BJJ specific' the better). Studies show that by doing S&C you reduce your risk of acute injury by 30% and overuse injuries by 50% which is huge. 

As far as steroids are concerned, I think that this is an issue for high-level competitors but will be essentially a non-factor for the everyday hobbyist and something that shouldn't really be dwelled on for most people IMO. I personally am against PED usage in BJJ completely, and I think as a community we have the power to impact change in the long term if it's something we are collectively against.

The disappointment to getting submitted by a blue or even a white belt is just not worth risking another devastating injury that could sideline you for months.

text:
Is BJJ Worth All Injuries? No—unless you’re a professional athlete or an MMA fighter. If your goal is to train for fun, maintain longevity, and stay in good shape, it doesn’t make sense to risk serious injuries like torn ligaments or damage to your neck. I’ve trained in boxing, Muay Thai, Sambo, and BJJ, and I can say BJJ tends to be far more traumatic. The injuries go beyond simple bruises and can be worse than those in striking martial arts. My own BJJ training schedule often looked like one week on, followed by two weeks of recovery, then starting over.
BJJ is certainly a practical and efficient martial art, but if you want athletic longevity, it might not be the best choice.

text:
My kids learn Muay Thai and western boxing for striking, wrestling and jiujitsu for ground confidence, and judo for transitioning between the two. We don’t emphasize anything high level. Just master four basic principles of each martial art. I really mean master it. 
Must Thai: perfect punch, elbow, knee, and kicking technique.
Wrestling/Jiujitsu: chokes, arm/leg locks/bars, take down offense and defense. 
Judo: four basic throws. 
It’s for self defense not competition in our house. 
If they want to compete they can lick a discipline and go for it, but regardless everyone has to MASTER those basic things in those specific disciplines. 
I subscribe to the idea that I’d more fear the person that has practiced a single move a thousand times, than a hundred moves one time.
I enjoy judo the best at my age now. When I was younger I preferred striking.

People from other arts endlessly malign the BJJ guard, and while it obviously is not a very practical or recommendable strategy to pull guard in MMA or self defense the majority of the time, it is still well within the realm of possibility that you will trip and fall, be taken down, be attacked while sitting down, or countless other such scenarios. A lot of the time, standing up may be a superior option to entering a confrontation on those terms, but that is not guaranteed to be either possible or ideal. 
 For this reason, I think it is good that despite the stigma, there are people in BJJ who spend so much time developing and exhibiting strategies which begin from open guard. It is not a comprehensive self-preservation strategy, but it's usefulness as a skill depends as much on the circumstances of the confrontation as it does with striking, wrestling, running, shooting or parkour.

text:
Tony
Love your boxing videos.

I personally think that Bjj is not a very practical art for self defense particularly in a street fight scenario where the surface is hard concrete, uneven, scattered with broken glass, stones etc.
Getting your opponent to the ground with the hope of securing an armbar, triangle or RNC  will get you injured before you do any damage to your adversary due to the surface you are fighting on.

The practical aspects of Bjj for the street would be, knowing how to fall (breakfall),  takedown defense, defense against a standing a choke, but these can be learnt from wrestling with the exception of choke defense.
So I would say boxing with some good takedown defense and maybe the ability to take someone down is mostly what you need.
In the ring or on the mat is a different story, where a grappling art will likely prevail most of the time.
Just my 2 cents.

The real risk of sunk-cost fallacy means that if people start in a useless martial art they end up feeling stuck in it even after realising it’s a waste of time and money. After investing so much on the road to a black belt, they feel they need stick with it to at least say they’re a black belt.

If they start in a martial art without a belt system, like boxing or wrestling, there’s no such problem. They learn something useful, can quit at any time and won’t have lost anything as the focus the entire time is on becoming effective in competing against other people, not a belt colour which in kids classes really has little value yet the kids are misled to believe it makes them effective fighters.

When Krav Maga was developed, it wasn't meant to be a style. It was a group of people training for survival, using whatever effective technique they could find. The training was pretty much MMA with street mindset: "we use what works, dump the rest". Therefore they sparred a lot, and were strong dedicated fighters.

The only Krav Maga that is actually worth something today (with rare exceptions) is the military version, because soldiers are not afraid to train the hard way. 

Honest observation from an active KM practitioner since 2009.

I've trained my fair share of Krav Maga. Real KM is not beautiful, technical, masterful and precise. It's violent, dirty, ugly, sloppy and chaotic.

Sloppy you say? Yes. In a rl situation, things get sloppy. My training companion and I would always do our best to mimic rl situations. Instructors would drill military stress situations constantly. It took me a lot of time to control the "freeze" phase of stress.

If you a watch video with a complicated technique, that's not "pure KM", that's new-age-fancy-KM. Remember, this system was created to fight a war in the middle of the desert. 

Things to keep in mind:
- You'll always get cut in a knife fight and your chances of survival are slim
- Disarming an opponent ONLY works if the opponent is not set to kill you, otherwise you're dead already (robbery, assault, etc.)
- Gun disarm is a russian roulette. You go for it and hope for the best.

These are some of the things that I've been taught by my KM instructors, who were either military or police.

His experiences as a doorman in London for many years also gave him background (and scars) in realistic knife defense vs what is seen in a lot of demonstration. Unfortunately, the quality of KM depends mostly on the individual instructor, since there is no single dedicated curriculum to test. It became popular and commercialized too quickly, much like CrossFit and now BJJ.

text: The thing with such practices such as Krav Maga and other systems that include prepared movements is that usually they are not made to "fight", but more to control, disarm or neutralize attackers. I think it's important for all martial artists to differentiate when to use what. This is also an integral part of martial arts.

Any time I hear "complex moves" in the context of Krav Maga, I cringe a little. In the Krav Maga training I had, the focus was simple techniques applied with controlled aggression. Lots of sparring, lots of force on force, and an emphasis that Krav wasn't about having a skill to skill fighting competition with your attacker, but how to get out of a bad (and unavoidable) situation quickly. If you have no choice but to fight, these are the risks, here are some solutions to get you through it. 

One good way our instructors made it clear that there are no "series of moves" that always work" is having us gradually increase the amount of force being used in any given scenario, and having us switch up training partners at some point. What was working with this guy, won't work at all with the next guy and so on. 

I've definitely seen some of the more questionable Krav Maga training online, and I'm lucky that the  place I used to train did none of that nonsense.

And what I've found is that all instructors were themselves accomplished martial artists before they started Krav Maga. Anyone who was somewhat adept in another art would do okay in Krav Maga. But people who have never done any martial art will mostly suck as a fighter practicing just Krav Maga. Unless the instructor teaches the basics from (kick)boxing and grappling, you will not become a good fighter.

Krav Maga is not intended to teach you to fight another accomplished fighter. But there simply is no replacement for sparring and other forms of stress testing.

text: Krav Maga actually means CONTACT COMBAT, not CLOSE COMBAT. The best school in L.A. is Krav Maga Worldwide which was founded in the 1990's by Los Angeles District Attorney, Darren Lavine. They have 2 locations, West L.A. and Sherman Oaks. Darren studied directly under Imi Lichtenfeld, the creator of Krav Maga. Krav Maga is not a MARTIAL ART, it's a FIGHTING SYSTEM, which basically means they adapt techniques from various martial arts. Other than weapon take-away defenses, you'll find a lot of western boxing, BJJ and Muay Thai. I always feel that people who say 'MMA guys would beat Krav guys' are kind of missing the point. I mean, of course they would. 

Krav is mainly meant to get yourself out of a dangerous situation, either by de-escalating the situation or by countering an attack and then getting the hell out of there after throwing at most three punches and a kick to create an opening to run. It's not meant to lead to a prolonged fight, and if you do end up in one, you're basically fucked, especially if it's against multiple people.

MMA, by contrast, is meant to be used in prolonged fights. Escaping isn't the object, but defeating your opponent within a specified rule set is. You're always in open combat, and always focused on the one person you're fighting. 

If you put practitioners of both in a room and tell them to fight, then probably the person who's always training for just such a situation is going to come out on top.

All of that said, I'd rather not get into a fight with either a well-trained MMA fighter or a well-trained Krav practitioner. Either would demolish me.

I would go for Dutch style kickboxing rather than muy thai MT is a beautiful art with powerful kicks and strikes and heavy clinch work and ellbows, but it’s built around engaging in exchanges. You *communicate* with your opponent you kick, they kick, you block, they counter. It’s rhythmic and power-based, and you're grounded in close range.

Dutch kickboxing took the foundations of MT (especially the low kicks and ellbows and clinch) but evolved it into a faster, more mobile, in-and-out system. Dutch fighters are lighter on their feet, throw quick boxing combinations ending in low kicks, and rely less on standing and trading. It’s more pressure based and fluid, less about waiting for a return exchange.

Historically, the dutch actually trained in mt in the 70s then blended it with western boxing (which is always good) and kyokushin karate that’s why their footwork, angles, and combo flow are so different.

So yeah, MT might hit harder, but dutch-style kickboxing moves smarter.

So I rather go with that. I train it myself for years and I really like being mobile wouldnt trade it. Still I respect the power of muy thai trust me I do.

pretty good video, and as a tkd instructor and as someone who competed for years, I will agree with many of your points. One cralification i would like to add though is how points are scored in sparring, and how it has changed in the past 15ish years. In modern tkd sparring (olympics) the hogu (chest protector) has pressure censors in it to auto add point when the amount of force passes a certain threshold, so weak kicks will not score. This however had the unfortunate side effect of changing what moves are effective, and making it look (and feel tbh) like tag with your feet.  
Prior to about 2010-2012ish tkd sparring was a lot more "physical" and had a lot more knockouts.  A large majority of non-olympic level tkd athletes agree, this older style was much better, and more "realistic".  The amount of knockouts, tkos, and even a few broken ribs I witnessed in this era can easily attest that tkd kicks are far from weak.
